documents.body:
S: About 6 weeks of the chest tightness coming on more often - now with brisk walking on flat ground, not just the reservoir hill, 3-4 times a week. Same pressure feeling, eases within a few minutes of stopping. Never at rest, never woken him. No dyspnea at rest, no palpitations, no syncope. Belly much better with small meals, weight back up to 75.

O: vitals charted. Heart regular, no murmur, no rub. Lungs clear. No edema.
ECG: NSR, no ST changes, no Q waves.

A/P: stable angina occurring more often, no rest pain. Hasn't seen his cardiologist in over a year. Referral back to cardiology, they can see him next week. Reviewed ED precautions for pain at rest or lasting more than 15 minutes. Continue aspirin, statin, amlodipine, lisinopril.

Outside cardiology - 01/18/2024

Mr. Graves returns after more than a year with exertional chest pressure that has become more frequent over the past two months, now with level walking. Symptoms resolve with rest in minutes. No rest angina.

Meds: aspirin 81, atorvastatin 40, lisinopril 20, amlodipine 5, prednisone 10, tamsulosin 0.4.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: BP and HR as recorded. Regular rhythm, no murmur. Lungs clear. Femoral and distal pulses intact.

ECG from your office 1/9 reviewed: sinus, no ischemic change.

Impression: stable angina with increasing frequency on medical therapy. Given his vascular history I favor going straight to coronary angiography.
Plan: outpatient cardiac catheterization, scheduled 2/2. Hold no medications other than the usual morning-of instructions.

Cardiology

documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outside cardiology - 02/16/2024

Seen for left groin discomfort and swelling for two weeks, starting a few days after his 2/2 diagnostic catheterization through the left femoral artery. That study showed moderate nonobstructive coronary disease with no lesion needing intervention; medical therapy continues.

He has CAD on chronic prednisone for GCA. Pain is mild. No leg swelling, numbness or coolness.

Vitals within normal limits.
Exam: small tender mass at the left groin access site with a palpable thrill and a continuous bruit. Distal pulses intact. Rest of exam unremarkable.

Labs: Hb 14.2, WBC 7.5, platelets 250, creatinine 1.0, BUN 18.

Arterial duplex of the left groin today: a small arteriovenous communication between the left common femoral artery and common femoral vein. No pseudoaneurysm. No hematoma of significance.

Impression: post-catheterization left femoral arteriovenous fistula, small.
Plan: observation, as many close on their own; repeat duplex with his vascular surgery surveillance. Return sooner for enlarging swelling, leg swelling or pain. Continue aspirin. Angina medical therapy unchanged.

Cardiology

documents.title: Emergency department record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER - EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
Arrival: 04/07/2024 13:20

CC: two weeks of feeling unwell, belly pain, painful purple legs, vision episodes.

HPI: 71 y/o man with GCA on prednisone, CAD, and a left groin AV fistula after a femoral cardiac catheterization 2/2. Over two weeks: progressive malaise, vague abdominal pain, a painful purplish discoloration of both legs, and several brief episodes of blurred or patchy vision in either eye lasting minutes. No headache, jaw claudication or scalp tenderness.

Meds: aspirin, atorvastatin, lisinopril, amlodipine 5, prednisone 10, tamsulosin 0.4. NKDA.

Exam: BP 155/90. Diffuse blanching erythematous rash over both legs with livedo reticularis; several toes dusky/cyanotic, pulses palpable. Fundi: bright refractile plaques within retinal arterioles bilaterally. Abdomen soft, mild diffuse tenderness.

Labs: creatinine 2.8 (baseline 1.2), BUN 50, CRP 15 mg/L, eosinophils 8% (absolute 700/uL), complement levels normal. UA: no protein; blood positive with 6-10 RBC/hpf.

MDM: livedo, blue toes, retinal cholesterol plaques, eosinophilia and kidney injury weeks after an arterial catheterization - cholesterol embolization syndrome. CRP only modestly raised and no cranial symptoms; GCA flare thought unlikely.

Disposition: admitted to medicine.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: hospitalist
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 04/07/2024  Discharged 04/12/2024

Principal diagnosis: cholesterol embolization syndrome (skin, retina, kidney) after femoral cardiac catheterization.
Secondary: acute kidney injury.

Course: supportive care. IV fluids, avoidance of further contrast and anticoagulants. Lisinopril held for the kidney injury. Aspirin and atorvastatin continued. Prednisone 10 mg continued unchanged; rheumatology was not consulted as there were no features of GCA activity. Creatinine peaked at 2.8 on arrival and was 2.3 on the morning of discharge with good urine output. Toe discoloration and leg pain improving. No further visual episodes.

Discharge medications: aspirin 81 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, prednisone 10 mg daily, tamsulosin 0.4 mg nightly. HOLD lisinopril until PCP review of kidney function.
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: PCP within 1 week with BMP.

Hospital medicine

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Hospital follow-up, 6 days after discharge for cholesterol embolization (rash, blue toes, retinal plaques, AKI) about 9 weeks after his femoral cath.

Feels better, more energy. Leg discoloration fading. Toes less painful, color returning. No more vision episodes. Eating ok, urinating normally. Off lisinopril since admission as instructed.

BP 146/86 off the lisinopril. Weight 74.
Skin: faint residual livedo both shins, toes pink, no ulceration. Pedal pulses palpable.
Heart regular. Lungs clear. No edema.
BMP today: Cr 2.0 (2.3 at discharge, 2.8 peak).

A/P
1. Cholesterol embolism with AKI - improving. Keep lisinopril held; it comes off the active list for now. Continue aspirin and atorvastatin. Avoid NSAIDs and contrast where possible. BMP in 3 weeks.
2. HTN - above goal off ACE inhibitor; accept for a few weeks while the kidneys settle, amlodipine 5 continues.
3. GCA - no flare features.
RTC 3 weeks.

reports.text:
Limited aortic and left groin duplex.
Aorta: infrarenal aneurysm, maximal anteroposterior diameter 4.9 cm (4.4 cm on CTA 08/2023). Proximal aorta and iliac arteries of normal caliber.
Left groin: small arteriovenous fistula between the common femoral artery and common femoral vein, unchanged in size. No pseudoaneurysm.
reports.conclusion: Infrarenal AAA 4.9 cm. Small left femoral AV fistula, unchanged.

documents.title: Vascular surgery follow-up
documents.author: vascular surgery
documents.body:
VASCULAR SURGERY - 08/20/2024

AAA surveillance. He had cholesterol emboli in April after his femoral catheterization, now recovered. No abdominal or back pain.

Exam: abdomen soft, nontender. Left groin with a soft bruit, no mass. Pedal pulses palpable, toes warm and pink.

Duplex today: infrarenal AAA 4.9 cm, up from 4.4 a year ago. Small left femoral AV fistula unchanged.

Plan: aneurysm has grown 5 mm in a year; repeat imaging with CT angiography in 9 months to plan for repair if it reaches threshold. Fistula: continue observation. BP control.

Vascular Surgery

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
AWV.

A heavy year: cath in Feb, groin AV fistula, cholesterol emboli with kidney injury in April. Recovered. Back to walking, tutoring starts again next month.
Functional status independent. No falls. Recall/clock normal. PHQ-2 1.
HCP on file.

Reviewed vascular letter: AAA 4.9 cm, CTA next spring. Fistula unchanged.

Exam: vitals charted. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft. Soft bruit L groin. Toes warm.

A/P
- HTN at goal on lisinopril 20/amlodipine 5.
- CAD stable on aspirin/atorvastatin.
- AAA, fistula: vascular following.
- Ischemic colitis: quiet.
- GCA: pred 10 per rheum, markers today.
- BPH: tamsulosin, good.
- Vaccines: flu, updated COVID and RSV with nursing next month.
Labs today. RTC 4-6 months.

GCA follow-up. Interval history notable for cholesterol embolization in April after a femoral cardiac catheterization, with transient visual episodes from retinal emboli, now resolved; not felt to be GCA. No headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or girdle symptoms.
